Oil biosynthesis in canola (Brassica napus); detailing the main metabolic steps from de novo fatty acid synthesis in plastids to triacylglycerol (TAG) assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)

Schematic representation of oil biosynthesis in canola (Brassica napus); detailing the main metabolic steps from de novo fatty acid synthesis in plastids to triacylglycerol (TAG) assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Plastidial Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDC) converts pyruvate into Acetyl‐CoA, followed by the action of Acetyl‐CoA Carboxylase (ACCase) to convert Acetyl‐CoA to Malonyl‐CoA. Malonyl‐CoA: ACP malonyltransferase (MCMT) further converts Malonyl CoA to Malonyl ACP, followed by elongation and reduction reactions catalyzed by Fatty Acid Synthase (FAS) to produce C16:0 and C18:0 ACP chains, which are then desaturated by Stearoyl‐ACP Desaturase (SAD) into C18:1ACP. These acyl‐ACP chains are hydrolyzed by thioesterases to release free fatty acids, which are later activated to acyl‐CoA by Long‐chain Acyl‐CoA Synthetase (LACS) and transported to ER. The acyl‐CoA pool (in step 7) acts as the central substrate source for TAG assembly via the Kennedy pathway. Other than direct incorporation (7a), It receives elongated products such as very long‐chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) including erucic acid by the Fatty Acid Elongase complex 1 (FAE1) action (7c), and FAD2/FAD3‐desaturated acyl chains (7b) transferred from PC through Phosphatidylcholine Diacylglycerol Cholinephosphotransferase (PDCT)‐mediated exchange (8). Arrows specify the direction of metabolic flow, with enzymes (represented by triangles) indicated at relevant steps
